newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Computer snafu again plunges Mir into crisis.
newsitem.headline: Computer snafu again plunges Mir into crisis.

text.p: A computer failure aboard the ailing Mir space station sent the ship spinning chaotically in orbit on Monday, forcing engineers to shut off all but vital life support systems, space officials said.
"We have turned off all energy-consuming equipment and only left life-support systems operational," flight director Vladimir Solovyov told reporters.
"With this computer fault today we are bracing ourselves for a tense situation with the battery buffers, our energy reserves," he said.
Mir's computer failed a few minutes before it docked with the Progress resupply ship, forcing its commander to dock manually at 4:53 p.m. (1253 GMT).

As the computer failed Mir also lost its orientation towards the sun, which the station's solar panels must face to create energy, Solovyov said. "There were no human errors in this situation. It was a technical malfunction," he said.

By late Monday, the Mir crew had fired off booster rockets to point it partially towards the sun, allowing the station to charge up its batteries before it attempts to reset the orientation early Monday.
"It would be better if you did this operation before 11 a.m. tomorrow. If the tests go through tomorrow we'll set up the orientation," flight director Solovyov told Mir during a radio link-up.
A computer breakdown a month ago sent Mir spinning for a day until the crew fixed it. That fault was caused by a cosmonaut who had mistakenly unplugged a key cable.
The latest in the seemingly unending wave of problems aboard Mir forced Mission Control to postpone vital repairs planned for Wednesday aimed at restoring energy to the 11-year-old station.

Mir has run on partial power since it collided with a previous Progress cargo ship on June 25 in the worst accident in its history. Several areas of the station have been out of action since then due to a lack of power.

"Unfortunately we have to move back repairs by two or three days," Solovyov said. "The repairs will be a five-hour-long operation and we cannot begin this operation without coming to terms with what has happened."
The Progress redocking was tense until the last few seconds, and poor visibility added to the woes of Mir commander Anatoly Solovyov, now on his fifth flight on the space station.
"I was actually impressed that Solovyov managed to dock the Progress with Mir in free drift; that's not an easy thing to do," said Bob Castle, a NASA space shuttle flight director.

After the redocking on Monday the atmosphere was tense at Mission Control. Top experts huddled to discuss the situation near the monitors of the operations centre, and sent up a rapid series of technical instructions to the crew.
"You need to pull out socket 20413. Pull it out carefully," a flight engineer told Mir.
On Sunday, the Progress redocking had to be cancelled because of a computer programming error on the craft.

Progress delivered oxygen, food, water and tools to Mir on July 7 and is now filled mostly with rubbish. Redocking a rubbish-filled module will provide better balance for Mir and will protect an uncovered hatch from prolonged solar exposure.
Progress undocked on August 6 to make room for a Soyuz spaceship bringing Solovyov and his flight engineer from Earth and has since been floating around some distance from Mir.
